title: "These Small Ones Dominate the Risk": Are Deadly 'Halloween Fireballs' Just Media Ghost Stories, or is the Cosmic Airburst Threat Real?
excerpt: A professor details the odds of a deadly Halloween fireball in 2026 and the serious damage such a rare cosmic airburst event could cause.
content:
A series of presentations at the Geological Society of America’s annual GSA Connects conference shows that media reports suggesting the 2026 fall Taurid meteor shower could include powerful “Halloween Fireballs” capable of melting everything on the surface below it are highly exaggerated.

“Scenarios in which large numbers of airbursts simultaneously rain down on the Earth, destroying cities across the planet and ending civilization, are science fiction,” conference presenter Mark Boslough, a Research Associate Professor of Earth and Planetary Sciences at the University of New Mexico, explained in an email to The Debrief.

However, the professor noted, a new analysis of such events, including the well-known “Tunguska” cosmic airburst that exploded over Siberia in 1908, suggests they could be even more devastating than previously believed, motivating researchers like himself to prepare for such “what-if” scenarios, however unlikely.

Halloween Fireball Cosmic Airbursts Are Real, But Rare

Earth crosses paths with the Taurid meteor stream twice a year, producing brilliant flashes of light in the sky. During the fall season, media reports often call these atmospheric meteor airbursts “Halloween Fireballs” because of their seasonal proximity to the spooky October 31st holiday.

Most Halloween Fireballs pose no real danger to people or structures on the ground. However, the 1908 crossing included what researchers believe was a “Taurid swarm.” One comparatively large object within that meteor swarm slammed into Earth’s atmosphere before exploding above the Podkamennaya Tunguska River region of Siberia in a brilliant fireball.

Although that cosmic airburst occurred over a relatively unpopulated region, the damage caused by the high-energy aerial explosion stoked fears that a returning Taurid swarm could deliver one or more life-threatening Halloween Fireballs in the future.

During his presentation, “Will Tunguska’s Evil Twin Return on Halloween 2026? Science and Skepticism in a Clickbait World,” Boslough highlighted the science behind the possibility, including the real potential return of a Taurid swarm.

For example, previously published models suggest the Taurid swarm is in an approximate 61-year resonance with Earth, placing the next event in 2030. However, the professor said the models also showed that the fall crossing would be 4 years earlier, “within a few weeks of October 31, 2026.”

This ominous date, combined with memories of Tunguska, has once again fueled fears and media speculation that this year’s Halloween Fireball swarm may include a hidden meteor that could cause a deadly cosmic airburst over a more populated region.

To address those fears, while also offering some hope that future events will help researchers spot potentially dangerous Taurid space rocks before they can cause any damage, Boslough reached out to The Debrief and helped separate media-driven ghost stories from potentially real Halloween horrors.

“Such Events Are More Dangerous Than We Had Previously Thought”

According to the UNM professor, new research has shed more light on the types of airbursts caused by Tunguska-type asteroids that “explode in the air but don’t hit the ground.” This includes supercomputer simulations by planetary defense researchers that have produced potentially horrifying conclusions.

“We have learned that such events are more dangerous than we had previously thought, because they are directional explosions,” Boslough told The Debrief.

In his presentation abstract, the UNM professor explained that the mainstream narrative for the past century has suggested that had the Tunguska space rock arrived 4 hours and 47 minutes later, it would have destroyed St. Petersburg. However, he added, while intentionally mimicking the clickbait style some media reports use to overstate the actual risk, “new orbital calculations have revealed the stunning truth.”

“If it had been mere minutes late, it could have destroyed a city in the US or Canada,” the professor explained. “A couple (of) minutes after that, it would have missed Earth altogether, only to return and menace our planet in the future. That time could be now.”

Boslough told The Debrief that if a Halloween Fireball-style cosmic airburst is large enough, it can incinerate everything on the planet’s surface directly beneath it “like a cosmic blowtorch.” He also noted that there are a million Tunguska-sized asteroids for every dinosaur killer, with most remaining undiscovered.

“One fear is that we still don’t know how many (if any) could be hidden in the Taurid stream that strikes Earth every year at this time,” Boslough explained, adding that “these small ones dominate the risk.”

The Probability is ‘Very Close to Zero’

Although scientists agree that another Tunguska-sized airburst is certainly possible, Boslough told The Debrief that the mathematical chances of a Tunguska-level event this October 31st are far lower than some more sensational media reports suggest.

“The probability that the Tunguska object had an evil twin that will create a cosmic blowtorch that destroys Denver (or any other city) on Halloween is very close to zero,” he explained, including the highly populated Colorado city as an example of the cities his team modeled for a possible airburst scenario.

Boslough said that such horrifying Halloween Fireballs events “are precisely the types of hypothetical scenarios we discuss at our Planetary Defense Conference every two years to practice our preparedness and mitigation planning.”

When addressing the chances of a Tunguska-level airburst scenario during the next Taurid swarms scheduled to swing by Earth six and ten years from now, respectively, the UNM professor’s conference abstract explained that the Taurid resonant swarm model does “predict close approaches of a hypothetical swarm in 2032 and 2036.”

Although the chances of a catastrophic Halloween Fireball during either event are also extremely low, the professor told The Debrief that a 2032 swarm could offer astronomers a chance to hunt for potential future dangers, including space rocks capable of producing deadly airburst scenarios.

“The good news is that new and more powerful telescopes for discovering and tracking asteroids will be in operation by 2032, when the next time the hypothetical Taurid swarm gets close to Earth,” Boslough explained,” and can provide advance warning if there’s a Tunguska-sized object on the way.”
